subject: Transport-layer options for Redwood Private (VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)
messages:

Subject: Transport layer options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Ava,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. We are starting the internal scoping for a Redwood Private deployment that will host PHI and payment flows; security and auditability are top priorities (HIPAA + some PCI scope). Our infra team is evaluating options for connecting our on-prem DCs (primary in us-east-1 / secondary in us-west-2) to the Redwood VPCs in the customer-managed AWS account.

High level constraints:
- ~200 RPS API calls at peak with occasional bursts (bandwidth spikes up to 400 Mbps).
- Target P99 latency <= 80ms for end-to-end inference.
- Need firm controls over routing / egress (audit logs), and avoidance of transitive routing that could expose internal networks.
- Prefer a solution that minimizes ongoing operational toil; we can tolerate some initial engineering work.
- Procurement is sensitive to recurring per-endpoint charges.

Can you summarize the tradeoffs between VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN for a setup like ours? Also: any hybrid recommendation (e.g., PrivateLink + VPN fallback) or alternatives like Direct Connect / Transit Gateway we should consider? If possible, please include expected timeline and cost direction of each approach.

Regards,
James
Head of Infrastructure, MedicoRe Health
security@medicore.com

From: Ava Chen <ava_chen@redwood.com>
To: James Smith <james.smith@medicore.com>
Date: 2026-12-10T10:07:00-05:00
Subject: Re: Transport layer options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi James — thanks for the clear context. High-level summary below; I also attached a one-pager that maps each option to compliance, latency, and operational burden. Happy to set up a call to walk through the details.

Quick comparison (short):
- VPC Peering:
  - Pros: Low latency, simple once set up, predictable cost (no per-endpoint LCU).
  - Cons: Cross-account peering is non-transitive and cannot peer across regions without extra hops (so multi-region becomes messy), potential route management complexity, and limited control over which resources are exposed. Not ideal if you want strict endpoint-level access control and no transitive exposure.
- AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints):
  - Pros: Endpoint-level access control (NLB -> interface endpoint), strong isolation (no transitive routing), integrates well with security reviews, and traffic stays on AWS backbone. Good for HIPAA because you can lock down service-identity.
  - Cons: Per-endpoint charges + NLB/LCU costs, slight increase in connection complexity, limits on simultaneous connections per ENI if not sized correctly. Cross-region requires separate endpoints per region.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec):
  - Pros: Fast to stand up, predictable per-hour cost, useful for initial PoC or fallback.
  - Cons: Higher jitter/latency variability, not SLA-grade for production without redundant tunnels/Direct Connect; more operational overhead on monitoring and certificate/PSK rotation.

Other options to consider:
- Direct Connect (with Transit Gateway): best for predictable high-throughput, lower egress cost at scale, but longer procurement and setup time.
- Transit Gateway + Direct Connect provides flexible hub-and-spoke for multi-region but adds cost.

Our suggested approach given your constraints: two recommended paths depending on appetite for runbook complexity and cost:
1) Enterprise (recommended for production HIPAA workloads with 400 Mbps spikes): Direct Connect + Transit Gateway into your AWS account, then Transit Gateway to Redwood VPCs or PrivateLink endpoints as needed. Pros: predictable bandwidth, lower egress unit cost at scale, stronger SLA. Cons: procurement lead time (2-8 weeks), circuit cost.
2) Accelerated secure path (recommended for faster delivery and strict isolation): PrivateLink for each region + redundant S2S VPN as backup. Pros: faster to deploy, endpoint-level isolation (good for audits), can be staged region-by-region. Cons: higher per-endpoint cost and per-AZ NLB overhead.

Next steps I suggest: 1) quick call to align on expected steady-state bandwidth and any procurement restrictions; 2) a mutual action plan with PoC milestones; 3) exchange AWS account IDs / ASN / proposed CIDR ranges so we can draft a configuration checklist.

Attaching: redwood-connectivity-onepager.pdf (high-level cost and diagram).

Forwarding James' note — MedicoRe needs guidance for HIPAA/PCI environment. My TLDR above. Internal asks:
- Marcus: can you sketch the 3-month TCO (PrivateLink per region vs TransitGW+DX) and call out NLB LCUs and endpoint-hour costs? They projected ~400 Mbps bursts and ~200 RPS.
- Priyom: any runtime considerations on our side for PrivateLink (ENI scaling, cert pinning, connection pools)? Also thoughts on offering a managed Direct Connect option vs just docs.

My recommendation: If customer wants lowest operational quarterly costs and they can tolerate procurement lead-time, steer them to Direct Connect + Transit Gateway (we can provide a managed onboarding checklist). If they want faster onset with strict isolation and security signoff, recommend PrivateLink (1 endpoint per region) + redundant S2S VPN fallback.

Risks/notes:
- VPC Peering is cheap performance-wise but cross-region and transitive limitations make it brittle for multi-region failover and for locked-down security posture. Also harder to provide
